titulo: Billy Graham · Preacher to the world

guion.texto: Washington, February 2018. In the Rotunda of the Capitol, where presidents have lain, rests the coffin of a preacher. It is plain pine, made by prisoners in a Louisiana penitentiary. He is only the fourth private citizen to receive this honor. His story began on a dairy farm in North Carolina, with a boy who milked cows at three in the morning.
William Franklin Graham Jr. was born on November 7, 1918, on a farm near Charlotte, four days before the end of the First World War. At home they called him “Billy Frank.”
His father, Frank, had only gone to school for three years, but he built one of the largest dairies in Charlotte. Billy milked from the age of eight and got up at three in the morning.
Every night at home, his father or his mother read the Bible aloud.
One spring day, Billy’s father lent a grove on the farm so that some businessmen could meet there to pray.
One of them, Vernon Patterson, asked God to raise up someone from Charlotte who would preach the gospel to the ends of the earth.
Billy, 15 years old, heard the singing from a distance as he pitched hay to the mules.
In 1934 Mordecai Ham, an evangelist from Kentucky, came to Charlotte. He preached in a wooden tabernacle with a sawdust floor, on the edge of town.
Billy went with his friend Grady Wilson. So that the preacher would not look straight at them, they joined the choir and sat behind him.
One night, at the end of the sermon, they sang “Just As I Am” and “Almost Persuaded.” On the last verse, Billy went forward. Grady went with him.
He was a week short of his sixteenth birthday. Twenty years later he remembered it like this:
I opened up my heart then, and knew for the first time the sweetness and joy of God, of truly being born again.
That night, when he got home, he told his mother:
Oh, Mother, I’ve been saved tonight.
After a single semester at Bob Jones College, where the rules were very strict, he arrived in 1937 at the Florida Bible Institute, near Tampa.
The institute was in an old Spanish-style hotel surrounded by a golf course, beside the Hillsborough River.
Billy practised his sermons on street corners, at a mission in Tampa… and, as he told it, before the fish and alligators of a nearby swamp.
One moonlit night in 1938, Billy went out onto the golf course. At the edge of one of the greens he knelt down.
“O God,” I sobbed, “if you want me to serve you, I will.”
In 1939 he preached his first revival, in East Palatka, and that same year he was ordained a Baptist minister.
That was the first little inkling I had that maybe the Lord could use me in evangelism.
In 1940 he entered Wheaton College, near Chicago. There he met Ruth Bell. She had been born in China, the daughter of medical missionaries, and dreamed of being a missionary in Tibet.
He graduated in anthropology in June 1943. On August 13 they married in Montreat, in the mountains of North Carolina, where Ruth’s parents lived.
Years later he said she was the one who had the greatest influence in urging him to be an evangelist.
In 1944 the singer George Beverly Shea joined him, and soon Cliff Barrows, who led the singing. With Youth for Christ, Billy preached all over the country.
In 1948, in a hotel in Modesto, California, Billy, Cliff, George and his friend Grady agreed on four rules. They did not write them down: they gave each other their word.
To be honest with money. To avoid even the appearance of evil. Not to criticize the churches, but to work with them. And not to exaggerate the numbers.
From that day on, I did not travel, meet or eat alone with a woman other than my wife.
In August 1949, at a retreat in the California mountains, a friend of his kept telling him that the Bible could no longer be believed as before. Billy was left full of doubts.
If I could not trust the Bible, I could not go on.
One night he went out into the woods, laid his Bible on a tree stump, knelt and prayed:
Father, I am going to accept this as Thy Word—by faith!
A few weeks later a campaign began in Los Angeles, in a great circus tent set up in a parking lot. The press called it “the Canvas Cathedral.”
The first week the tent was half empty. Billy and his team prayed to know whether they should go on… and they went on.
We’re living at a moment in world history in which God is giving us a desperate choice. And I believe the choice is either revival, or judgment.
In the third week, a reporter told Billy he had just been “kissed by William Randolph Hearst”: the Hearst newspapers began reporting the campaign across the country.
Among others, the cowboy singer Stuart Hamblen and the Olympic athlete Louis Zamperini came to faith.
The campaign was planned for three weeks and lasted more than eight.
In 1950 he founded his association and began a radio programme. In the American South, law and custom kept white and Black people apart.
In 1953, in Chattanooga, the organizers put up ropes to separate the seats of white and Black people. The head usher refused to take them down. Billy took them down himself.
As his son Franklin would remember it, Billy told them:
Either these ropes stay down or you can go on and have the revival without me.
He did not always stand as firm in other Southern cities. But as early as 1952 he had said: “There is no scriptural basis for segregation.”
In 1954 he came to London. Much of the British press mocked him before he even began.
For nearly three months he preached at Harringay Arena, an indoor stadium of some 12,000 seats. Cliff Barrows led the choir with his shining trombone; George Beverly Shea sang.
According to his team, some two million people heard him in those months. The closing meeting, at Wembley Stadium, gathered about 120,000.
If God should take His hands off my life, my lips would turn to clay.
In 1957 he preached at Madison Square Garden in New York for 16 weeks in a row. It had been planned for six.
That summer he called in public for laws against segregation, and added his first Black member to his team, Howard O. Jones.
On July 18 he invited the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to the platform. He introduced him like this:
A great social revolution is going on in the United States today.
King prayed for “a warless world” and for “a brotherhood that transcends race or color.” Afterwards he wrote to Billy:
You have courageously brought the Christian gospel to bear on the question of race.
Billy travelled the world. In 1973 he preached in Yoido Plaza, in Seoul, a former airstrip. His interpreter was the Korean pastor Billy Kim.
On the last night, according to his association, about 1,100,000 people gathered: the largest meeting of his life.
He travelled several times to Communist countries. In 1982 he said in Moscow that there was “a measure of religious freedom” there, and many criticized him.
In 1984 he toured the Soviet Union for twelve days. In 1992 he visited Pyongyang, in North Korea, where Ruth had gone to school as a girl, and preached in its churches.
In October that year he preached for three days at the Olympic Stadium in Moscow.
Three days after the attacks of September 11, 2001, the nation heard him at the Washington National Cathedral. He was 82.
I have been asked hundreds of times in my life why God allows tragedy and suffering. I have to confess that I really do not know the answer totally, even to my own satisfaction.
As a Christian, I have hope, not just for this life, but for heaven and the life to come.
In June 2005, at 86 and suffering from Parkinson’s disease, he preached his last campaign, in New York. He came to the pulpit with a walker.
He preached on Nicodemus, the man who came to Jesus by night:
“Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.” (John 3:3 · BSB)
Tonight, open your heart and say, ‘Lord Jesus, come into my heart’–and He will.
Ruth and Billy lived together for almost 64 years, in their home in the mountains of Montreat.
Ruth died on June 14, 2007, with Billy and their five children beside her. Billy said:
Ruth was my life partner, and we were called by God as a team.
On her gravestone, Ruth wanted a phrase she had seen on a roadwork sign:
“End of Construction. Thank you for your patience.”
In his last years he could barely see or hear, and seldom left home. He had said:
I look forward to death, with great anticipation. I’m looking forward to seeing God face to face.
He died at his home in Montreat on February 21, 2018. He was 99.

His funeral was held in a tent, like the one in Los Angeles in 1949. He was buried beside Ruth, in a prayer garden in Charlotte, the city where he grew up. According to his association, more than 200 million people heard him preach in person, in more than 185 countries and territories. His gravestone says only: “Preacher of the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ.”
“I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.” (John 14:6 · BSB)

Sources: the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association and the Billy Graham Library, TIME (1954), PBS, Christian History, Christianity Today and the King Institute at Stanford University. Billy Graham’s words are quotations from his published sermons, interviews and writings.
